stages.credit: The Veil · Advaita Kelkar + Faith Andrew
intro: The first proposal develops a place for learning, making and gathering inside Habersham Hall. Early research asks how a student-led atelier can connect the campus and the city, and how one space can support exhibitions, events, workshops and everyday encounters.

The Veil translates that brief into translucency, layered enclosure and a visible frame. Under the idea “From Containment to Creation,” the former jail becomes a setting for creative exchange. Precedent studies lead into concept renders, fabrication studies, floor plans and a sectional proposal.

pages.label: The Threshold Atelier · page 10
text: SCAD Design Build is an adaptable pavilion platform for creative collision. Designed for events, exhibitions, and spontaneous gatherings, this student-powered community workshop exists under the Savannah sky—a porous stage for learning, making, and public exchange. Neither fully inside nor outside, campus nor street, this space is intentionally open and in flux. Here, architecture meets performance, critique meets celebration, and the city is invited to witness and join the creative process.

intro: The next stage brings The Veil and Prism together. The Veil’s work on enclosure and reveal meets Prism’s focus on community and artistic expression. The proposal develops into Unveil: an arrival sequence that connects the historic building, shared workspaces and a central gathering space.

Entry, zoning and programme diagrams test how people move through the site. Plans, sections and perspective studies develop the relationship between the existing masonry, the new interior volume and spaces for collaboration.

groups.title: Unveil design development
groups.note: From the project’s Unveil presentation folder.

intro: The full studio develops one proposal for Habersham Hall: a new auditorium and atelier within the historic enclosure. A floating volume above a reflecting courtyard brings gathering, presentation and reflection into one section.

The proposal connects water management with a transparent healing envelope, a ventilated buffer and a glazed roof shaded by a scrim. Mass-timber trusses and steel tension rods form the proposed structural system. The final presentation brings together the design narrative, environmental strategies, material choices, plans, sections and construction details.

pages.label: Design pillars · slide 10
text: 01 Ghosts of the Past Existing Enclosure

pages.label: Site conditions · slide 11
text: The existing Habersham Hall is a Moorish Revival-style three story stucco building originally from the 1800s. The building contains a former residence hall, with 27 former prison cells which frame a 5,250 sqft open-air courtyard. This building was the former Chatham County jail and features its iconic onion-shaped dome, which replaced its original octagonal Byzantine style tower. Throughout its lifetime, the site received a renovation to create 117 more cells in 1886, its tower replacement in 1898 due to a fire, the demolition of the roof in 1984, and renovations in 2007 to the jailer residence and tower. SCAD acquired the property in 1989, from an owner that had intentions to turn the jailer's residence into a bed and breakfast. Today, the intention is to turn the existing jailer's three-story residence to six rooms to serve as an Atelier and 200 seat auditorium. The first floor of cells would turn into bathrooms and a gallery space, with the second and third floor of the existing cells to serve as studio spaces for the Atelier. The open-air courtyard would host an innovative auditorium, which would also feature classroom space. Two cells on the northwestern facade would turn into an interior stairwell, with another stair at the southwestern facade on the exterior of the building, which keeps the courtyard free of stair circulation. The introduction of an elevator makes the Atelier and the rest of Habersham's courtyard accessible. Currently, there is an inaccessible ramp that brings one from the parking lot, to the first level of the former residence on the eastern facade. The existing entrance that is on-grade to the parking lot, opens into a ramp to bring visitors down three feet, where the courtyard floor is. The majority of the current site is impermeable paving, including the parking lot, and the open-air courtyard. To contrast this, visitors would enter at the level of the reflection piazza, aligning their first view with the proposed water feature. From the entry, the circulation branches off in three directions: the auditorium at the right, the preserved cells, studios, and restrooms directly ahead, and the new Atelier to the left.

pages.label: Orientation and landscape approach · slide 12
text: The eastern facade features 18 metal latticed windows and frames the parking lot. The diagonal patterning on the latticed windows is original and would remain, but the orthogonal grate would be removed. This is the facade that features the front entry to the new Atelier and would feature the main entry to the new design. The Atelier space is south of the open-air courtyard. The northern facade of the courtyard features a large metal latticed window, and an on-grade entrance off the parking lot. The 27 cells are within the western facade, which borders Colonial Park Cemetery.

The design concept involves a flooded condition, in which there is a recessed reflecting pool to address a conversation of sea level rise. This also would serve as a water management system for stormwater retention, to reduce peak runoff during heavy rain events. The water strategy would also recycle greywater and reuse water as part of the building systems. This takes the design into the 21st century, for a transparent solution about construction vulnerability with climate change. Due to the existing site being impermeable, the goal would be to reintroduce plant life to Habersham Hall. In the open-air courtyard, one can already see examples of nature growing within the walls.

pages.label: Grading concepts · slide 13
text: The site currently has an entry above the ground of the courtyard at plus seven feet off grade. The open-air courtyard is recessed into the ground by four feet, so the current conditions are not accessible. Meaning, the first floor of the Atelier is eleven feet above the recessed courtyard floor, which itself is three feet below grade. A new entry off the eastern facade would open at the level of the grade, which is the same level that the first level cells are at. This would fill in the recessed courtyard to meet the grade. The existing variance in grading creates an opportunity to have a ramp at the primary entrance that goes up to the second floor of the cells. This variance also naturally lends itself to orienting the stage of the auditorium to the northern portion of the site, as the existing conditions naturally dip towards the north, which would accommodate sight lines of guests. The 'floating' design becomes a metaphor for reintegration and elevation, symbolically lifting up the human spirit, which is the antithesis of its former use as Chatham County Jail.

pages.label: Schematic management and setback context · slide 14
text: The design solution is offset by five feet from the existing walls of Habersham's open-air courtyard, due to structural engineering recommendations to stay off the existing walls. This incorporates a ghost of the past, as one of the major renovations of Habersham included offsetting a new addition eight feet off the existing walls. Furthermore, structural engineering has recommended the design as a whole should help to brace the northern and eastern facade as these walls are unsupported. This offset condition allows for the design to take advantage of passive cooling by creating a stack ventilation and heat chimney condition at the five foot interstitial space with operable glazing for exterior walls. This involvement of natural ventilation, beyond providing access to fresh air, helps to mitigate the fact that in 1978, the jail was condemned partially due to lack of natural daylight and poor ventilation. The auditorium is essentially a 'building within a building' and this concept can actually find its roots in a major renovation in 1886, which led to the cell layout seen today. The auditorium can seat 200 people, a recall of the hundreds that used to be imprisoned in Chatham County Jail. The module for the new building is based on the existing conditions, which show about 14 feet on center of each pilaster of the cells. This 14 feet, split into four equal parts, is three and a half feet. In several ways, the new design ties back to the existing conditions, the rich patina and layered history of the site, and creates a stage to celebrate SCAD's innovation.

pages.label: Water stewardship and stormwater retention · slide 15
text: The project incorporates a comprehensive water stewardship strategy that focuses on reducing potable water demand, improving stormwater management, and promoting responsible reuse of water resources within the built environment. The system is designed to manage water as a valuable resource rather than a disposable utility, integrating stormwater retention, greywater recycling, and water reuse to create a more resilient and efficient building water cycle. These strategies work together to reduce strain on municipal infrastructure, mitigate urban flooding, and lower overall water consumption.

A key component of the water management approach is stormwater retention designed to serve the scale of an entire urban block. Rather than allowing rainwater to immediately enter municipal storm systems, the project incorporates systems that capture, store, and slowly release stormwater. This approach reduces peak runoff during heavy rainfall events and helps mitigate the burden placed on urban drainage infrastructure.

pages.label: Greywater recycling and water reuse · slide 16
text: Stormwater retention may be achieved through a combination of below-grade storage systems, permeable surfaces, landscape infiltration areas, and roof drainage capture. Water collected from roof surfaces and hardscapes is directed into retention systems where it can either infiltrate slowly into the ground or be stored for later reuse. By managing stormwater at the building and site level, the design reduces the risk of localized flooding and contributes to improved water quality by limiting polluted runoff entering nearby waterways.

Complementing the stormwater strategy is a greywater recycling system, which captures water from sinks, showers, and other non-potable interior sources before it enters the wastewater system. This water is filtered and treated to a level appropriate for non-potable reuse applications within the building. Greywater recycling reduces the demand for treated potable water while also lowering the volume of wastewater discharged to municipal systems.

pages.label: Closed-loop water strategy · slide 17
text: Once treated, recycled greywater is reused within the building for non-potable functions such as toilet flushing and irrigation systems. Bathrooms are one of the largest sources of potable water consumption in most buildings due to the water required for flushing fixtures. By supplying recycled greywater for these functions, the system significantly reduces the amount of potable water required for daily building operations.

Together, stormwater retention, greywater recycling, and water reuse create a closed-loop water management strategy that reduces potable water consumption while improving resilience to changing climate conditions and urban water demands. This integrated approach allows the building to operate more efficiently within the larger urban water system while contributing to responsible long-term resource management.

pages.label: High-performance healing envelope · slide 18
text: At the core of the building strategy is a high- performance "healing" envelope designed to act as an environmental mediator between exterior climate conditions and interior conditioned spaces. Rather than functioning as a static barrier, the envelope operates as a dynamic system that actively regulates thermal transfer, solar exposure, and daylight penetration. Multiple layers of protection and environmental control, including a double glass skin façade, insulated roof glazing assemblies, and continuous insulation systems, work together to improve overall building efficiency while maintaining interior comfort.

A key component of this system is the double glass skin façade. The façade consists of two layers of glazing separated by a ventilated cavity that functions as a thermal buffer zone. The outer glazing layer serves as the primary weather barrier, protecting the inner façade from wind, precipitation, and temperature fluctuations. The cavity between the two layers moderates heat transfer and improves façade performance across seasonal conditions.

pages.label: Double-skin ventilation and thermal comfort · slide 19
text: During cooler periods, solar radiation entering the cavity warms the air within this intermediate space, creating a greenhouse effect that helps reduce heating demand. In warmer conditions, the cavity can be ventilated to exhaust accumulated heat before it reaches the interior, reducing solar heat gain while maintaining access to daylight. This strategy stabilizes interior temperatures and improves occupant comfort by limiting drafts and temperature fluctuations near the perimeter of the building.

The roof assembly further enhances envelope performance through the use of triple-insulated layered roof glazing. This system introduces controlled daylight into interior spaces while maintaining strong insulation values. Multiple glazing layers separated by insulating cavities limit heat transfer while allowing diffused daylight to enter the building. Supporting these systems are high-performance envelope assemblies designed to minimize thermal bridging and uncontrolled air infiltration. Continuous insulation, coordinated air barriers, and vapor control layers work together to maintain consistent thermal performance and prevent moisture migration throughout the building envelope.

pages.label: Passive and low-energy systems · slide 20
text: The overall design prioritizes passive performance in order to reduce operational energy demand before relying on mechanical systems. By emphasizing envelope performance, solar control, and airtight construction, the building minimizes heating and cooling loads while maintaining stable interior environmental conditions.
Airtightness is a critical component of this strategy. Even small gaps in the envelope can significantly increase heating and cooling demands. By designing a continuous air barrier and

penetrations throughout the building envelope, uncontrolled air exchange is reduced and the efficiency of mechanical systems is improved. These assemblies are designed to exceed minimum code requirements and support long-term reductions in operational energy use.
Dynamic solar control is provided through electrochromic glazing systems. Electrochromic glass adjusts its transparency in response to solar

intensity, time of day, and interior comfort needs. As solar radiation increases, the glazing darkens automatically to reduce glare and limit solar heat gain. When solar intensity decreases, the glass returns to a clearer state, allowing greater daylight penetration.

This responsive shading strategy stabilizes interior temperatures and reduces reliance on traditional shading devices such as blinds or louvers. By controlling solar heat gain more precisely, the electrochromic system reduces peak cooling loads and improves overall occupant comfort while maintaining balanced daylight conditions within interior spaces.

pages.label: Renewable energy integration · slide 21
text: comprehensive approach to reducing operational energy demand. The building envelope actively moderates thermal transfer while responsive solar control technologies help maintain stable interior conditions throughout the year.

By minimizing heat gain, reducing air infiltration, and maximizing daylight availability, the building reduces reliance on mechanical heating and cooling systems. This approach improves long-term building performance while lowering operational energy consumption.
The integration of advanced façade systems, high- performance glazing assemblies, and
solar control technologies allows the building to maintain high levels of occupant comfort while operating with significantly lower energy demands. This strategy supports long-term durability,
establishes a resilient building framework capable of adapting to changing environmental conditions.

pages.label: Water feature — overview · slide 23
text: The flooded courtyard at Habersham Hall transforms the historic jail's interior void into a spatial and environmental narrative about resilience, memory, and adaptation. In coastal cities like Savannah, where increasing storm surge and sea level rise threaten the urban fabric, the project imagines a future in which architecture does not resist water entirely but learns to coexist with it. The courtyard is intentionally flooded, filling the space between the basement level and the first level of the existing cell block.

This body of water becomes both a literal and symbolic datum: a calm reflective surface that represents the rising waters projected for coastal environments while supporting a new architectural intervention that hovers above it. Suspended over the water, the auditorium volume reads as a vessel —an elevated program that acknowledges the inevitability of flooding while demonstrating how architecture can adapt by lifting itself above vulnerable ground conditions.

pages.label: Waterproofing approach · slide 24
text: Technically, the flooded courtyard functions as a controlled water basin constructed within a concrete shell at the basement level. The basin is designed to hold water permanently up to the level of the existing cells at +7 feet, requiring a layered waterproofing assembly to protect the structural slab and adjacent spaces. Beneath the visible courtyard surface, paving sits on a pedestal or mortar bed above a sequence of filter fabric, drainage mat, protection board, and a continuous waterproof membrane applied over a primed structural concrete slab. This layered system ensures that water remains contained within the basin, while allowing drainage and maintenance access beneath the finished surface.

At the entry piazza, glass walls define the boundary between the partially submerged exterior approach and the interior circulation space. These walls are waterproofed on the exterior face so that the water can visually extend to the building edge, while maintaining the integrity of the occupied spaces behind it. The result is a courtyard where the water line becomes a visible architectural threshold, reinforcing the project's relationship to flooding as both condition and design driver.

pages.label: Filtration system · slide 25
text: Within this basin, water quality and clarity are maintained through a reflection pool filtration system designed at the scale of a large architectural water feature. Mechanical filters remove debris and suspended particles, while saltwater filtration prevents algae and bacterial growth to preserve the reflective quality of the surface. Circulation pumps move water continuously through the filtration network, and make-up and overflow systems regulate the water level as evaporation or rainfall changes the basin volume.

These mechanical components are located in a dedicated equipment vault adjacent to the courtyard, allowing the water to remain visually calm while the technical infrastructure remains hidden. Maintaining a clear reflective surface is critical to the spatial experience: the water acts as a mirror that doubles the surrounding architecture and heightens the perception of the suspended auditorium above.

pages.label: Spatial organization around flooding · slide 26
text: WATER FEATURE SYSTEM SPATIAL ORGANIZATION AROUND FLOODEI

The spatial organization of Habersham Hall responds to the flooded courtyard so that water becomes the central orienting element of the project. Visitors enter at the level of the reflection piazza, aligning their first view with the water's surface before choosing their path through the building. From this point, circulation branches in three directions: to the right toward the auditorium, straight ahead toward the preserved cells, studios, and restrooms, and to the left toward the main house and secondary classroom spaces.

This moment of arrival places occupants directly at the threshold between land and water, reinforcing the project's conceptual stance that future architecture must negotiate changing environmental conditions rather than ignore them.

pages.label: Water and architecture · slide 27
text: WATER FEATURE SYSTEM CONNECTION TO ARCHITECTURE

The spatial relationship between water and architecture ultimately carries the deepest symbolic meaning of the intervention. By hollowing out the base of the former jail and allowing the lowest level to be reclaimed by water, the project removes the physical space that once represented the deepest point of confinement and isolation. In its place, the flooded courtyard becomes a reflective void-both a memorial to the building's past and a projection of environmental futures. Above this surface, the auditorium volume floats as a new communal space, embodying reintegration and elevation.

The suspended architecture metaphorically lifts the community above the history of incarceration that once occupied the same footprint, while simultaneously modeling how buildings in coastal regions may need to rise above projected flood levels. In this way, the project frames water not only as a threat but also as a catalyst for architectural transformation, demonstrating how historic structures in places like Savannah can evolve to meet the environmental realities of a rising sea.

pages.label: Building section — water and envelope · slide 28
text: HABERSHAM HALL 235 HABERSHAM ST. SAVANNAH, GEORGIA MARCH 11, 2026

pages.label: Building section — new and existing · slide 29
Double-skin envelope · slide 30
text: Glass Box - Structure The primary architectural intervention is a transparent glass enclosure that sits within the historic shell of Habersham Hall. Rather than attaching directly to the masonry walls, the glass envelope is supported by its own independent structural frame. Columns are positioned within the rhythm of the existing bays, allowing the new structure to align with the proportions of the historic architecture while remaining visually minimal. This hybrid structural system supports large spans of glazing while preserving open views across the space. Because the structural frame is anchored to its own foundation system rather than relying on the historic walls, the existing building remains structurally untouched. This separation protects the historic fabric from additional loads or structural alteration while allowing the new envelope to perform according to contemporary building standards. The glass itself should be double thick panes, with thermally broken aluminum mullions. The curtain wall will attach to the mass timber structure through the use of extension poles, allowing the glass to be pulled completely away from the structure.

Glass Box - Environmental strateg Environmentally, the glass enclosure acts as the primary thermal barrier of the new interior space while maintaining visual transparency. High-performance glazing allows natural daylight to pass through the façade while limiting excessive solar heat gain. During the day, light filters through the enclosure and illuminates the historic surfaces within the courtyard, transforming the cavity into a softly lit gallery that reveals the texture and materiality of the original building. At night, subtle interior lighting allows the historic structure to glow through the glass volume, reinforcing the layered relationship between the contemporary intervention and the preserved architecture. Rather than replacing the historic façade, the glass envelope acts as a protective veil that mediates between the interior environment and the surrounding climate.

pages.label: Scrim shading · slide 31
text: Shading-Structure Above the roof structure, an exterior shading system composed of operable scrim panels provides an additional environmental layer. Structurally, these scrims are supported by a lightweight framework positioned above the glass roof, allowing the shading system to function as a secondary skin that floats above the enclosure. This elevated placement ensures that the shading system intercepts sunlight before it reaches the glazing surface while maintaining a minimal visual presence within the architectural composition. The scrims should be almost entirely opaque but allow some filtered light to pass through. This, mixed with the UV resistance in the glass will block almost all of the heat and solar radiation that could permeate into the space.

Shading -Environmental strategy The scrim system plays a crucial role in regulating solar exposure within the space. The operable panels can extend during warmer months to block direct solar radiation and prevent heat buildup within the glass enclosure. Because the shading occurs outside the glazing, solar energy is stopped before it enters the building, significantly reducing interior heat gain. During colder seasons, the scrims can retract to allow sunlight and warmth to penetrate the enclosure, supporting passive solar heating when it is beneficial. In addition to moderating temperature, the scrims diffuse incoming light, reducing glare and creating softer daylight conditions within the interior. This filtered lighting improves visual comfort and ensures that the space remains functional for presentations, gatherings, and daily use.

pages.label: Five-foot buffer · slide 32
text: Buffer - Structure Between the historic walls and the glass enclosure lies a five-foot buffer zone that becomes a critical spatial and environmental layer within the project. Structurally, this separation allows the new building to exist independently within the historic shell while maintaining a continuous cavity between the two systems. The historic structure therefore continues to act as an outer boundary while the new envelope defines the interior conditioned spaces. This gap preserves the integrity of the historic walls while introducing a flexible environmental layer that can accommodate airflow, lighting, and maintenance access. Within this glass enclosure is a nana-wall system that allows the entire space to be opened to the outdoors. Th doors would be able to collapse down to fit at the front and back of the space.

Buffer - Environmental strategy Environmentally, the five-foot cavity acts as a climatic mediator that stabilizes conditions between the exterior environment and the conditioned interior. The space reduces direct exposure of the glass wall to solar radiation and weather fluctuations, allowing temperature changes to occur more gradually across the envelope. The entire glass box is elevated above a shallow pool of water within this zone, introducing an additional passive cooling strategy. As air moves across the water's surface, evaporation naturally lowers the temperature of the surrounding air. This evaporative cooling effect helps regulate the temperature within the cavity between the two building skins. Cooler air generated at the surface of the water rises upward into the buffer zone and circulates through the enclosure, contributing to a passive cooling cycle that improves interior comfort while reducing reliance on mechanical systems.

pages.label: Roof envelope · slide 33
text: Roof - Structure The roof is designed as an operable system that supports natural ventilation throughout the enclosure. Openings at the roof level allow warm air that accumulates within the glass volume to escape upward. As heated air rises and exits through these operable panels, cooler air is drawn upward from the lower levels of the enclosure. This process creates a natural stack effect that encourages continuous airflow through the building envelope. When combined with the cooling air produced within the buffer zone, the operable roof establishes a passive ventilation cycle that regulates temperature and improves air circulation throughout the space. By allowing heat to escape before it accumulates, the system reduces the cooling load on the building and supports a more energy-efficient interior environment.

Roof - Environmental Strategy The roof structure requires greater structural support than the vertical glazing system and therefore introduces a hybrid structural solution. Columns positioned between the existing bays carry the load of the roof system while maintaining large spans of glass between structural members. This arrangement allows the roof to remain visually light while providing the stability required to support operable components and shading systems above. By aligning the columns with the existing architectural rhythm, the new structural elements integrate with the historic building without overwhelming it visually.

pages.label: Interior finishes — material palette · slide 35
text: The interior finishes of the auditorium are designed to support acoustic performance while reinforcing the material atmosphere of the space. Wood, fabric, and acoustic panel systems are used throughout the seating area to reduce sound reflection and maintain clarity within the room. These materials work together to absorb excess sound while maintaining a cohesive interior palette.

Perforated wooden backrests are integrated into the seating design to support sound absorption within the auditorium. The small perforations allow sound waves to pass through the outer wooden surface and into the acoustic foam located behind the panel. Rather than reflecting sound back into the room, the foam absorbs the sound energy, helping reduce reverberation and improve overall acoustic quality within the theater.

The seating risers are constructed with perforated plywood acoustic panels backed with sound absorption batts. These panels allow sound waves to enter the perforations and dissipate within the insulation layer behind them. This system helps control echo within the stepped seating area and distributes acoustic absorption across the auditorium floor surfaces.

pages.label: Interior finishes — acoustic and material strategy · slide 36
text: Auditorium seating is constructed with high-density molded foam cushions upholstered in thick v

contributes to sound absorption while providing comfortable seating for occupants. The fabric upholstery is finished in a soft light blue tone, referencing the flooded courtyard imagery that informs the conceptual design of the project.

Wood panel baguettes are incorporated along portions of the ceiling and wall surfaces. These vertical wood elements create a layered surface that allows light from the glass roof system to pass through the gaps between panels. This condition helps diffuse incoming daylight while maintaining visual warmth within the interior.

At the 2nd landing, a glass floor panel introduces a moment of transparency between levels of the building. The structural glass allows light to pass through the floor plate and illuminate the space below. As occupants move across the landing, their movement is visible from below, creating silhouettes that emphasize activity and spatial connection within the building.

The auditorium is equipped with an audiovisual system designed to support a 200-person theater environment. A large LED screen provides a clear visual display for presentations and performances, while integrated speakers distribute sound evenly throughout the seating area. These systems support the functional performance requirements of the auditorium while integrating with the overall interior design.

pages.label: Sustainable goals — water, energy and landscape · slide 37
text: Water stewardship is not only one of the main components of the project's overall mission and message. It is a central driver of the project's environmental strategy, treating water as a visible and regenerative resource rather than a disposable utility. The design integrates a comprehensive water management system that captures, retains and reuses water across the entire urban block. Greywater generated from sinks and other non-potable sources is captured and treated on site, then redistributed for restroom flushing and landscape irrigation. This system significantly reduces reliance on potable water and is designed to achieve a 40-50% reduction in potable water consumption. Permeable surfaces and planted retention areas allow stormwater to infiltrate slowly into the ground, improving water quality and supporting groundwater recharge. These strategies transform the landscape into an active infrastructure system that both manages water and enhances the ecological performance of the site.
A high-performance envelop environmental comfort while demand. A double-skins faça glazing and electrochromic s gain, and thermal performan

Passive design strategies reduce reliance on mechanical systems and lower energy consumption. Natural ventilation, energy recovery systems, and daylight harvesting work together to improve indoor comfort while minimizing operational energy use.
A green roof system supports stormwater management, improves thermal performance, and provides habitat. Native plantings increase biodiversity while reducing irrigation and maintenance requirements.

pages.label: Sustainable goals — materials and adaptability · slide 38
text: The building utilizes a mass timber and FSE wood structural system to reduce embodied carbon. Adaptive reuse strategies and construction waste recycling further support responsible material use.

Bicycle parking facilities encourage active transportation, while electric vehicle charging stations support cleaner mobility. These strategies promote sustainable commuting and reduce reliance on conventional vehicles.

pages.label: Roof structure and assembly — overview · slide 39
text: The proposed roof encloses the former courtyard of Habersham Hall to create a covered auditorium while referencing the spatial volume of the historic jail room that once occupied the site. Rather than reconstructing the original enclosure, the new roof establishes its height and profile through a contemporary structural system. The geometry of the structure traces the scale of the former room while remaining clearly legible as a modern intervention within the historic masonry courtyard.

The enclosure is formed as a glazed roof supported by a mass timber structural framework. This approach preserves visual access to the sky while providing weather protection and environmental control for the auditorium below. The transparency of the roof maintains a sense of openness within the courtyard while establishing a defined interior space suitable for gathering and performance.

pages.label: Roof form · slide 40
text: Roof Structure and Assembly | Roof Form

The roof is organized as a pitched gable rising to a central ridge. This sectional profile establishes the primary interior volume of the auditorium and corresponds to the approximate height of the former jail room. The sloping planes define the enclosure of the space while maintaining a light structural presence above the surrounding masonry walls.

The pitched geometry also supports environmental performance. Rainwater is directed toward the perimeter of the roof where it is collected through integrated drainage systems. The angled surfaces allow daylight to enter from above and distribute evenly across the seating area, supporting natural illumination within the space.

pages.label: Timber trusses and steel tension rods · slide 41
text: Roof Structure and Assembly | Structural System

The primary structure consists of mass timber trusses spanning the courtyard and supported by columns positioned along the perimeter walls. The trusses support the glazing system and carry environmental loads including wind and precipitation. These loads travel through the rafters toward the ridge and down into the supporting columns.

Because the sloped roof geometry produces horizontal thrust at the supports, a steel tension rod connects the lower portions of the trusses. The rod operates in tension to resist these outward forces and stabilize the structure across the span. Adjustable connections allow the tension rod to be calibrated during installation. Steel node connections occur at both the ridge and the eaves.

pages.label: Structural glazing system · slide 42
text: Roof Structure and Assembly | Structural Glazing System

The roof enclosure is constructed using a four-sided structural glazing system supported by aluminum glazing rails mounted above the mass timber trusses. The glazing assembly is positioned approximately 7 inches above the structural members, creating a continuous cavity between the truss and the glass.

Insulated laminated glass panels are bonded along all four edges using structural silicone. This method eliminates exterior pressure plates and produces a continuous glass surface with minimal visible framing. Separating the glazing from the structural frame allows the glass system to accommodate small

pages.label: Ridge ventilation · slide 43
text: Roof Structure and Assembly | Ridge Ventilation

At the ridge, the glazing system is terminated with a continuous cap element running along the peak of the roof. This cap integrates a series of small operable windows that allow warm air to escape from the highest point of the auditorium.

As air within the space warms, it rises toward the ridge and exits through these openings. This condition creates a natural stack ventilation effect that promotes airflow through the enclosed courtyard and improves interior comfort. The ridge cap also protects the glazing joints from direct rainfall while maintaining the continuous profile of the roof.

pages.label: Exterior scrim and double-skin assembly · slide 44
text: Roof Structure and Assembly |Exterior Scrim and Double-Skin Assem

A metal scrim layer is installed above the glazing system to provide solar shading. The scrim is positioned approximately 12 inches above the interior face of the glazing, creating a ventilated cavity between the two layers.

Together, the glazing and scrim form a double-skin roof assembly. The inner glazing layer functions as the primary enclosure while the outer scrim layer filters incoming solar radiation. The ventilated cavity allows heat to dissipate before reaching the glass surface, reducing solar heat gain within the auditorium. This layered configuration maintains transparency while introducing an additional environmental control layer above the roof.

pages.label: Interior light control · slide 45
text: Roof Structure and Assembly |Interior Light Control

Additional solar control is provided by Baguettes louvers mounted along the interior face of the mass timber trusses. These louvers attach directly to the inside of the glazing members and run perpendicular to the rafters.

The system uses wooden baguettes measuring approximately 2 inches in width. Their spacing allows them to intercept direct sunlight entering through the glazing while maintaining diffuse daylight within the auditorium.

Integrating the louvers within the truss depth aligns the shading system with the structural rhythm of the roof and allows daylight conditions within the space to be moderated without obstructing views through the glazing.

pages.label: Roof drainage system · slide 46
text: Rainwater is managed through an integrated gutter system located along the perimeter of the roof. The pitched structural glazing directs water by gravity across the glass panels toward the eaves. At the roof edge, the glazing terminates above a concealed aluminum gutter built into the roof assembly, allowing runoff from the glass to drop directly into the channel.

From the perimeter gutters, water is conveyed through downspouts concealed within the supporting columns and directed to the site stormwater system. Integrating the gutters and downspouts within the roof and structural system allows the glazing to maintain a clean, uninterrupted appearance while providing reliable drainage.

pages.label: Structural system — modular framework · slide 47
text: The reinvention of Habersham Hall begins with the establishment of a rigorous structural grid, a move that serves as both a nod to the building's storied past and a blueprint for its adaptable future. While the original masonry shell tells a story of static weight and historical permanence, the new intervention introduces a 27-foot modular sub-grid derived from the building's existing 14- foot structural spans. This framework does not merely dictate the placement of physical elements; it creates an intellectual order that allows the building to breathe and evolve.

the structural grid acts as a liberating force. By aligning columns, structural bays, and circulation
consistent framework, the design ensures that future programmatic shifts, whether they be educational, civic, or exhibition-based, canbe accommodated without

compromising the architectural integrity of the whole. The grid is the silent coordinator of the space, ensuring that as the needs of the Savannah community change, the building remains a functional participant in civic life rather than a rigid relic.

pages.label: Structural system — water · slide 48
text: At the heart of the design is a profound spatial gesture: the primary gathering hall is conceived as a floating timber volume, suspended with ethereal lightness above a ground- level reflecting pool. This move serves a dual purpose, both environmental and symbolic. By introducing a water plane beneath the central span, the design effectively pulls the exterior entry piazza into the heart of the building.
This interior water featurel ac ng and

mirror. It cools the microclimate of the hall through evaporative cooling, a critical consideration in the humid Savannah climate, while simultaneously amplifying the natural light that pours in from the atrium above. Visually, the pool blurs the boundary between the solid floor and the liquid surface, creating a "spatial hinge" where the architecture seems to hover. This elevation of the communal space is not merely an aesthetic choice; it is a symbolic elevation of the community itself, lifting the site of collective learning above the very element, water, that the building seeks to study and address in the context of rising sea levels.

pages.label: Structural system — truss system · slide 49
text: The structural transition from the masonry past to the timber future is achieved through a sophisticated mass- timber truss system. These trusses, aligned precisely with the 27-foot primary grid, utilize a hybrid material logic to achieve long-span efficiency. By reinforcing the timber members with high-strength steel tie rods, the design achieves a delicate balance between compression and tension.
The steel rods serve a vital mecr

the lateral thrust generated by the gabled roof, allowing the timber chords to remain remarkably slender. This "tectonic honesty" ensures that the structural members do not become overbearing or bulky. Instead, they appear as a rhythmic series of light, linear elements that march across the ceiling plane. This system allows for a 48-foot clear span, creating a vast, column-free interior that is essential for the building's role as a lecture hall and exhibition space. Here, the architecture is not just a container for activity but a visible demonstration of engineering craft, where the relationship between the warmth of the wood and the precision of the steel is laid bare for the observer.

pages.label: Structural system — prism and atrium · slide 50
text: To protect this intricate timber skeleton while maintaining a sense of openness, the design employs a transparent glass envelope. This skin does more than provide a thermal barrier; it acts as a vitrine that showcases the internal structural logic to the surrounding city. A glass gable roof, situated at the ridge of the building, forms a luminous atrium that draws daylight deep into the interior volume, reaching even the lowest levels of the reflecting pool.

visually permeable, breaking down the traditional "black box" of institutional architecture. From the street, the activity within the gathering hall, the movement of people, the play of light on the water, and the intricate web of the trusses, is visible to the public. This creates a "civic theater," where the act of learning about environmental impact becomes a visible part of the urban fabric. The glass gable specifically references the original form of Habersham Hall, reinterpreting the historic roofline through a contemporary lens of lightness and clarity.

pages.label: Structural system — civic space · slide 51
text: The project's social heart is the elevated presentation stage and gathering space. Positioned strategically above the entry piazza, this area functions as a social hinge. It is the point where the private, internal world of research and study meets the public, external world of the city. By elevating this program, the architects have created a vantage point that allows occupants to look out over Savannah, connecting the internal discourse on sea-level rise with the actual geography at risk.

modular seating and stepped platforms that follow the structural grid. These elements wrap around the reflecting pool, creating a flexible forum that can be used for formal lectures or informal reflection. In this environment, the architecture becomes a "spatial instrument." Every element, the rhythm of the columns, the sound of water, the filter of light through the glass, works in concert to heighten the occupant's awareness of their environment.

pages.label: Structural system — adaptable framework · slide 52
text: The intervention at Habersham Hall ultimately transcends the traditional definitions of historic preservation. It is a project that views "structure" as more than just a means of holding up a roof; it is a means of holding up a community's future. Through the integration of the modular grid, the long-span timber trusses, and the symbolic use of water, the building is transformed into a visible framework for environmental awareness. As Savannah faces the mounting challenges of coastal flooding and sea-level rise, Habersham Hall stands as a testament to the power of adaptive reuse. It is a building that celebrates the craft of construction and the clarity of light, serving as a beacon of collective learning. It is no longer a static artifact of the past,
architectural organism, one that is as resilient, transparent, and adaptable as the community it serves.
